Yann LeCun has changed the game for robotics.

Research he co-authored tackles a problem inside AI world models: their internal representations can make planning harder than it needs to be.

A world model predicts what happens after an action. But even useful visual features can form curved paths in its internal “map,” making distance to a goal misleading.

The researchers introduced Temporal Straightening.

During training, it encourages those internal paths to become straighter, so the planner gets a more useful measure of progress.

The results:

More stable gradient-based planning
Higher success rates across tested goal-reaching tasks
Code available for others to explore

The approach changes how the model represents movement, rather than rewriting every RL algorithm to work in curved space. 

For robotics, that’s a useful direction: build world models whose internal maps help an agent choose its next move.

A new study in Science argues that the next major glaciation had already begun roughly 2,000 years ago, before modern warming reversed the trend in the 20th century.

The evidence comes from the Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island, the last surviving remnant of the enormous Laurentide Ice Sheet that once covered much of Canada and reached as far south as Illinois.

Because Barnes is frozen directly to its bedrock, advancing ice buries and preserves vegetation beneath it. Researchers radiocarbon dated plants emerging as the ice retreats to reconstruct its history.

They found that after melting to a minimum extent around 3,000 years ago, the ice began expanding again about 2,000 years ago. The researchers interpret this as the earliest stage of the next glacial period.

Left to natural orbital cycles, that cooling would have unfolded extremely slowly, potentially taking tens of thousands of years to rebuild a continent spanning ice sheet.

The Barnes ice cap may now disappear entirely within the next few centuries, removing the final remnant of an ice sheet that repeatedly served as the nucleus for much larger glaciations.

I used to be the person companies called after they got hacked.

And I noticed something early on.

The hack almost never sank them. The cover-up did.

Every time, the team’s instinct was the same: wait until we know more, wait until we're sure, wait until we have the perfect statement, etc.

And some of the biggest companies in the world have learned what that waiting costs.

In 2016, Uber got hacked. Instead of telling anyone, it paid the hackers $100K to delete the data and stay quiet, and labeled it a bug bounty. The truth came out a year later. Uber paid $148M to settle with all 50 states, and its former security chief was criminally convicted.

That same year, Yahoo revealed that a 2014 breach had exposed 500M accounts. The news landed in the middle of Verizon buying the company. Verizon cut $350M off the price.

And in 2017, Equifax discovered a breach affecting over 140M Americans, then waited 40 days to tell the public. During that window, an executive who'd figured out what happened sold nearly $1M in stock. He went to prison for insider trading.

Meanwhile, hackers don't wait. They post your data. They email your customers directly. And when customers hear it from a stranger first, that trust is gone for good.

Telling customers early doesn't mean admitting fault. It can be as simple as: "We found suspicious activity. We're investigating. Here's what you should do right now. We'll update you as we learn more."

On Tuesday, I'm sharing the exact framework I'd use to write that email if I were in your shoes. Follow and turn on notifications so it's there when you need it.

Customers will forgive you for getting hacked. Most of them expect it by now.

What they won't forgive is finding out you knew and said nothing.

University of Texas paper finds that handing small memory decisions to a fast scoring model let an AI memory system build its memory of long conversations 6.6 times faster

Many memory systems ask an LLM to make small choices, like what to link or when to stop searching.

Generating text for each choice is slow, and those calls pile up during memory building and search.

Jev-Mem gives those choices to a fast scorer, Jev, that returns probabilities in batches instead of text. The LLM is called only at the end, to read the chosen memories and answer.

On the LoCoMo long-conversation benchmark, it got a 0.777 answer score versus 0.700 for the best baseline. It built memory in 158 seconds versus 1,044 for the fastest rival and answered in 0.93 seconds versus 1.47.

If your memory pipeline calls an LLM for routing, scoring, or stopping, try a fast classifier there and save the LLM for answers.

Most founders think cold email is dead.

We've sent 10M+ of them and built $70M+ in pipeline.

10 things that still work in 2026:

1) Delete the unsubscribe link from every cold email

Write "if you don't want more emails, reply 'banana' and I'll stop" instead.

Every opt-out comes back as a reply, and spam filters read replies as engagement (keep the link on your newsletter).

2) Test the offer before you touch the copy

The same script on the same inboxes can book 1 lead per 25 contacts or 1 per 10,000, depending on the offer.

3) Put a number from their business in the email

A campaign using {PROJECT} and {LOCATION} variables hit a 14.5% reply rate, while the same script without them sat at 1-3%.

Our AI-written first lines hit 0.27%.

4) Email the info@ and personal addresses too

One local list gave us 3,621 business emails and 4,553 personal or info@ ones.

The personal ones booked a lead every 55 contacts, and the business ones needed 95.

5) Qualify the list before you pay to enrich it

> AI summary of every company
> ICP agent scoring fit (and what disqualifies)
> cut anything under 80%
> then run the email waterfall

Raw Apollo pulls land at 50-60% qualified, and this gets you to 90-95%.

6) Cut every company that isn't running ads

Your list shrinks about 30% and reply rates double, because a company paying for ads already has budget for growth.

7) Send one follow-up, then move to new contacts

Nobody wants a fourth "Hi John???" in their inbox.

Put 80% of daily volume on people who've never heard from you.

8) Answer every positive reply inside 5 minutes

2114662858399044071.text:
Shallom nigga. It's been a while. 

Here's 15 laughably powerful persuasion and behavioral sceince principles that you can immediately implement to print more money from your ads, your funnel, your emails, your content, etc. 

You can just copy and paste this post into whatever agent  you use for your copy, create a checklist and tell it to audit its output  against it the checklist. 

Do it RIGHT NOW nigga don't delay. 

Alr here we go: 

1. Identity mirroring. Everyone has an identity that they project internally and externally.
And 9 times out of 10 these identities are idealized versions of who they THINK they should be. 
Humans have consistency bias, which means they want to act in a way that ALIGNS with the identity they hold.
If you have a strong understanding of the identities that your avatars and sub-avatars internalize then you can literally call them out in your copy and mirror them so that your sales argument is something that THEY NATURALLY ALLIGN WITH.
Example 1: survival niche
Avatar 1: 40-60 year old men with families, conservative, traditional values.
Identity/identities: providers, protectors, man of the house, etc.
Mirror: “True protectors take action to keep their families safe.”

Example 2: B2S info/ coaching offer.
Avatar: young, self-made entrepreneurs
Identity: driven, successful, hard-working.
Mirror: “Every success entrepreneur took a huge risk that ended up paying off.”

You can apply around with these mirrors and then use them as a base for your actual copy.

2. Perception IS reality. If your market believes that all gurus are scammers then that is the reality that YOU as the marketer now reside in. 
Your job is to understand which perceptions stand in the way of your sales argument and which perceptions can actually HELP you. 
It takes good instincts to know which is which. 
This is why in depth avatar research is so fucking important because you need to understand the ETHOS of a given market (will go in-depth on this in a later post). In the example I made, you don’t try to convince them that not all gurus are scammers. 
Maybe you could do that but it’s less efficient. 
It’s way easier to just position yourself as being anti-guru. 
You hate gurus too. 
You aren’t a guru. 
Which is funny because some of the biggest info clingers on the planet use this principle. 

3. People act out of sub-conscious emotional triggers and use logically acceptable NARRATIVES based on their biases & desires to justify that decision. 
The best copywriters understand the core desires and use language that hijacks the prospects existing logical narrative to push a point home. 
This is where marketers fuck up, your prospects don’t need an objective logical analysis of the decision, they need a statement that SOUNDS logical/ socially acceptable to them.
Example: AI offer.
Core emotion: FOMO. **THIS IS WHAT THEY ACT ON
Logical narrative the prospect uses to justify the action: "The economy is shifting, and AI is changing everything. If I don't buy into this masterclass/tool right now, I’m going to get left behind. It’s irresponsible not to have this."

4. Justification looping. Every single thing that you say needs to be logically, intuitively justifiable by your prospect. Most people stop at justifying their mechanism, justifying claims about why things their market has tried didn’t work, all the basic shit. 
But have you justified your offer? 
Why are you giving them such a “no-brainer” offer? 
If you have urgency elements in your copy/ on your lander, have you explained WHY this is urgent? 
If you introduce scarcity, do you have an actual reason why this is scarce? 
You need to understand that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. If you don’t provide that evidence then your prospect will automatically call bullshit.

5. The way you say something can be more important than the thing you say, especially when you have a skeptical/ highly sophisticated market (I’ll get to this in a second). 
This is obviously specific to video ads/ VSLs, good example was the yapper ad trend. If you look at some of the most popular yappers (ads and TikTok shop videos), the delivery in terms of the pacing, tonality and cadence is all intentionally trying to lower your guard and make you feel like this is just another video on your feed. 
Another good example is Tony Robbins. When he needs to drive a point home he increases his volume, he using pauses to give you space to digest his point. Now imagine for example you’re scripting an ad for a marketing offer to a skeptical, sophisticated market and you want to take the angle of other market agencies being scammers. If your vocal DELIVERY in that ad doesn’t match the premise of what you’re trying to say, your market is going to immediately reject you.

6. People believe that their situation is unique. And they’re looking for reasons why your offer WOULDN’T work for them. 
The most common obstacle that occurs in a sales process is some version of “Will this work for my specific situation”. 
If you’ve ever been in a sales org you know this. 
You need to go through your market research flows and make sure you have enough data for a deep understand of the unique situational constraints that your market has (both real and perceived). 
Make a list, have AI order them by commonality then audit your ads, VSLs and landers and ask yourself if you’re overcoming the most common ones.
 Are you overcoming them at all? 
Are there any constraints that would be specific to an angle you’re running that you haven’t even mentioned in the ad? (This is a very common mistake).

7. Human behavior is ultimately driven by three fundamental psychological needs:

Autonomy: The deep desire to be the author of one's own life, free from constraint.
Competence: The urge to feel effective, skilled, and capable of overcoming challenges.
Relatedness: The craving for belonging, status, and connection within a tribe or peer group.

These core needs directly influence people’s motivators when the actualization of any of those needs is threatened. 
"Competence" example: “I’ve been trying to make my ads work for weeks I need to figure this out”. This is their CONDITION. And they naturally become receptive to any message that aligns with that condition.

And so to align with that condition you can make them feel competent by telling them that they already have the skills, they already have the knowledge, they’re just missing one small thing that will make it all click. This kind of narrative is literally EVERYWHERE, especially in the online marketing/ coaching space. If you want to do more autism research into this just loop up “Self-Determination Theory, Dr. Edward L. Deci”

8. Dimensionalization. You want to use words that burrow into people’s brain and infect it with your message. Notice the words I used. “Infect” “burrow”. It FEELS like some foreign parasite taking control. 
Doing this is simple: take any vague, abstract line of copy (especially when describing a problem or making a change-state claim) and think “how can I make someone feel, see, hear, smell, taste this idea”.

9. Associations can be more powerful than outright declarations.
Think about the supplement offers like turmeric pills that claim that ancient cultures used the core ingredients for their gut health (or whatever). 
Association with ancient cultures = healthier, more natural. 
Second-order assumption = this product is healthier and more natural. 
Now take shit like bull testicle pills for testosterone. Association with bulls = high testosterone, high vitality. 
Second-order assumption = this product will increase my testosterone. 
It doesn’t even matter if it’s true or not, the association did all of the selling for you. 
Another example: Amazon FBA mass market bizop. Association with Amazon: Amazon is a massive, billion dollar business. 
Second-order assumption: If I sell on Amazon there’s a high likelihood that I’ll make money. 
Here’s the thing, you can exploit this even if you’re selling a product/ service without an obvious association. I like to do this by taking whatever my core methodology (or mechanism) is and connecting a specific aspect of it to an anchor (a key figure/ thought leader, a company, a culture) that my market idolizes. Example: I’m selling a metal focus offer to entrepreneurs. Entrepreneurs idolize Elon Musk. Elon Musk uses “algorithmic thinking”, which my offer teaches. Notice how this is different from authority proof (which a lot of people implement) since we aren’t claiming that the anchor actually used the product. They don't need to because the ASSOCIATION is just as powerful.

10. The second your ad appears on someone’s feed, that person’s brain is subconsciously looking for ANY reason to ignore you. 
The brain is bombarded with millions of stimuli every single day. To actually PAY ATTENTION to a stimuli, the brain has to expend a ton of energy. 
And since the brain wants to conserve energy, it decides to filter out what it predicts as “sameness”. (Look up the reticular activating system (RAS) if you want to go into detail). 
The most effective way to bypass the RAS is by presenting an idea of reality that’s so bizarre, counter-intuitive, mysterious, unbelievable, offensive in your hook/ headline that the brain can’t PREDICT what’s about to happen.
Here are some common copy frameworks for this:
a. The hidden mechanism/ weird culprit: “This buried IRS loophole lets real estate investors save 80% on their tax”/ “This banana is the real reason why your skin sags after 50”

b. Statistical impossibility : “This 4-word email generated $575,789”

c. Attacking a universally accepted rule in your market (one of my personal favorites): “Testing more creatives is killing your brand” “Moisturizing your skin every night is giving you more acne” “Here’s how eating pizza for lunch can help you lose more fat than chicken and brocolli” (V-Shred printed multiple 9 figures on the back of this idea btw).

d. Herd-follower bias:“The top 1% of law firms are trying to keep Googles new “AI visibility” update a secret”

e. The unspoken truth: “here’s what the gurus refuse to tell you about starting an AI agency”

f. EXTERNAL CATALYST NIGGAAAA IYKYK (if you don’t know look up “catalyst hooks” on my page you’ll see a full guide : “This new Facebook ads update called sequence learning just killed creative testing” “

11. The fear of loss is more immediately motivating than the potential of gain. 
Simplest way to exploit this quickly is by taking any hooks you have running right now that are promise/ outcome/ benefit driven and flip the narrative to a negative. I’m running a hook rn that says “if you want your law firm to lose money you should hire an SEO agency” and it’s one of my top performers.

12. The best way to introduce a new/ novel concept I.e. in your UPM/ USM is a way that makes your prospect inherently understand it is by mapping an unknown concept to a known concept. 
You do this primarily using metaphors. 
The “known” part is determined by the sophistication of your market.
Unique problem mechanisms example for mass market joint supplement offer (just off the dome):
Novel concept: “Age-related joint degradation is caused by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) breaking down the extracellular matrix of cartilage faster than chondrocytes can synthesize new collagen.”
Re-written with a “known” concept: "Think of your knee joint like the door hinge. 
When that hinge is brand new, it opens and closes effortlessly because it has a rich layer of grease making everything glide smoothly.
Now, imagine what happens if you squirt a drop of acid onto that hinge every single day. That the grease dries up."...
"Most people think their knee pain is just 'getting old' or 'wear and tear.' But that’s dead wrong. 'Wear and tear' doesn't cause pain. Corrosive Enzymes do.
Inside your joint, your body produces tiny pac-man-like enzymes called MMPs. When you were 20, your body produced enough protective fluid to wash these enzymes away. But as you age, your joint stops producing that protective fluid. Those enzymes get trapped inside your knee joint, eating away at your cartilage like acid on a door hinge until your bones are grinding together with every step you take."

13. You must limit the cognitive load in your prospect as much as humanly possible. 
When someone is watching your ad, their brain is running on a very limited amount of energy. 
And if you exhaust that energy, the person is going to scroll. Cognitive overload does NOT mean too long. there are 45-minute VSLs pulling eight figures/month. Overload happens because of processing friction. There are a bunch of ways that you might be creating that friction but the two biggest offenders that I’ve seen: a. Too many overlapping ideas, outcomes, problems or mechanism drivers. These are some of the most cognitively “dense” parts of your message. And so when you keep adding more and more of each you’re just increasing the strain on your prospect’s brain. 
There’s a reason why most of the copywriting OGs taught to focus on ONE core idea, focus on ONE core reason why everything your prospects have tried before failed.
The second offender happens when there’s gaps in your argument that confuse the prospect to the point where they have to fill in the gaps. 
The simplest example happens when you don’t bridge certain blocks of copy properly or you just don’t include them in the first place. 
Example of no bridge: “Cold outreach is dead, use our AI software to close more deals.” 
With the bridge: “Cold outreach is dead because prospect inboxes are saturated with spam filters. 
Our AI bypasses inbox filters by simulating human writing patterns, dropping your message straight into the primary inbox where 90% of deals are actually closed.”

Now these gaps can be incredibly nuanced. An example of another gap: people have semantic associations. These are mental connections between two concepts that are wide spread across a population. Most people think of the liver as a “filter” or the brain as a “muscle” or memory as a “hard drive”. I’m going to use the liver as an example. Let’s say you’re writing about the forces of nature in your mechanism and you talk about the liver acting as a sponge. This might seem insignificant but when someone heard the liver acting as a “sponge” it clashes with their semantics which creates cognitive load.

14. Belief shifts. I hear people talk about it all the time but I haven’t heard a lot of people talk about how you ACTUALLY shift someone’s beliefs. 
You cannot attack a core belief head-on, or you trigger the backfire effect. 
This is a cognitive bias in which presenting a person with objective, undeniable facts that contradict their deeply held beliefs does not change their mind. 
You can spot this bias EVERYWHERE, in normie ragebait reactions, on gender discussion on Reddit, in the comments under your ads, political arguments etc.
Instead of attacking that belief, you VALIDATE it as being entirely logical based on their past evidence ("You're right to think cold email is dead, because the old spray-and-pray method was saturated"), and then introduce a narrow wedge that expands their paradigm. 
Mechanistic example: “That method is dead, but a hyper-segmented micro-channeling approach is getting agency owners a 20% reply rate right now”. 
External authority example: “But if cold email didn’t work at all then why are Fortune 500 companies spending million of dollars hiring people whose only job is to send emails?”
 When dealing with NEGATIVE identity-based beliefs i.e. “I’ll never lose weight” a good tactic is to externalize blame onto a third party aka the “common enemy” trope.
 Ex: “It’s not your fault. The reason why you aren’t losing weight isn’t because you aren’t disciplines enough or motivated enough. You were just fed a bunch of fad diets and useless at-home workouts by greedy fitness coaches.”

15. The best copy uses momentum to pull the reader to an inevitable conclusion. Joseph Sugarman (absolutely goated copywriter) called this the slippery slide. This is a measure of how well each core “block” of copy (i.e. promise, claim, mechanism, proof, catalyst, etc.) FLOWS from one to the other. I want you to read through the last ad script, VSL script, whatever you wrote and as you’re reading ask yourself: “is there any point where I suddenly jumped from one premise to another without establishing a clear bridge?” “Does each premise feel like a natural RESOLUTION to the premise that I established before?”
